docs.title: Pthread Library Lab Tutorial: Thread Creation and Synchronization (Enhanced)
docs.text: This lab tutorial will guide you through the fundamentals of using the Pthread (POSIX Threads) library in C++ to create and manage threads. We will explore how to create threads, pass arguments to them, and witness the power of parallelism. We will also delve into the critical concept of thread synchronization using mutexes to prevent common concurrency issues like race conditions.

docs.title: 1. Thread Creation
docs.text: In this section, you'll learn the basics of creating a new thread. Pthreads are a standard way to create and manage threads in Unix-like operating systems.

docs.title: What is a Thread?
docs.text:
A thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process. A single process can have multiple threads running concurrently, all sharing the same memory space. This means they share global variables, the heap, and file descriptors. However, each thread has its own private program counter, stack, and set of registers. This shared memory model makes communication between threads easy but also introduces challenges that we will address later.

The main thread of your program starts when main() is called. This main thread can then create other threads, which we'll call child threads. This process is often referred to as forking.

docs.title: Thread Forking and Joining
docs.text:
The lifecycle of a thread involves creating it (forking) and then potentially waiting for it to finish (joining).

  • Forking: The pthread_create function creates a new thread and makes it executable. The operating system's scheduler will then decide when to run it. After the call, both the original (parent) thread and the new (child) thread are running concurrently.

    Diagram: Thread Forking 

        Main Thread
         |
         |-------------+
         |             |
pthread_create()   New Thread starts
         |             |
 Continues execution   Executes its function
         |             |
         .             .
         .             .

  • Joining: A thread can wait for another thread to complete its execution by calling pthread_join. This is a blocking call. The thread that calls pthread_join will pause its execution until the target thread terminates. This is essential for ensuring that results computed by a child thread are available to the parent thread before the program exits.

    Diagram: Thread Joining 

        Main Thread         Child Thread
         |                   |
    (running)            (running)
         |                   |
 pthread_join(child) <---- terminates
         |
    (paused, waiting)
         |
    (resumes after child finishes)
         |
  Program continues
         |

docs.title: Creating a Simple Thread
docs.text:
To get started, you need to include the pthread.h header file in your C++ program.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

// The function that the new thread will execute.
// It must take a void* argument and return a void*.
void* myFirstThread(void* arg) {
    std::cout << "Hello from the new thread!" << std::endl;
    return NULL; // Threads must return a value (NULL in this case)
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread_id; // Variable to store the thread ID

    std::cout << "Main thread: Creating a new thread." << std::endl;

    // Create the new thread
    // It will start executing the `myFirstThread` function
    pthread_create(&thread_id, NULL, myFirstThread, NULL);

    // Wait for the created thread to finish its execution
    pthread_join(thread_id, NULL);

    std::cout << "Main thread: The new thread has finished." << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

Explanation:

  • #include <pthread.h>: Includes the necessary header file for Pthread functions.
  • pthread_t thread_id;: Declares a variable of type pthread_t, which is an opaque type used to uniquely identify a thread.
  • pthread_create(&thread_id, NULL, myFirstThread, NULL);: This is the core function for creating a new thread.
    • 1st argument (&thread_id): A pointer to the pthread_t variable where the ID of the new thread will be stored.
    • 2nd argument (NULL): A pointer to thread attributes. We pass NULL to use the default attributes (joinable, default stack size, etc.).
    • 3rd argument (myFirstThread): A pointer to the function that the new thread will execute.
    • 4th argument (NULL): A void* pointer to the argument that will be passed to the thread function. Here, we pass no arguments.
  • pthread_join(thread_id, NULL);: This function makes the calling thread (the main thread in this case) wait for the thread specified by thread_id to terminate. The second argument could be used to retrieve the return value from the thread, but we are ignoring it by passing NULL.

Sample Output:

Main thread: Creating a new thread.
Hello from the new thread!
Main thread: The new thread has finished.

docs.title: Passing Multiple Arguments to a Thread
docs.text:
The pthread_create function only allows you to pass a single void* argument. To pass multiple values, you must bundle them into a single object, typically a struct, and pass a pointer to that struct.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <string>

// A struct to hold the arguments for our thread
struct ThreadArgs {
    int id;
    std::string message;
};

void* printArgs(void* arg) {
    // Cast the void* back to our struct type
    ThreadArgs* args = (ThreadArgs*) arg;

    std::cout << "Thread ID: " << args->id
              << ", Message: " << args->message << std::endl;

    // It's good practice to free the dynamically allocated memory
    delete args;

    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread1;

    // Create a new ThreadArgs object on the heap
    ThreadArgs* args = new ThreadArgs();
    args->id = 101;
    args->message = "This is a message for the thread.";

    // Create the thread and pass the pointer to our struct
    pthread_create(&thread1, NULL, printArgs, (void*) args);

    // Wait for the thread to finish
    pthread_join(thread1, NULL);

    return 0;
}

Explanation:

  1. We define a struct called ThreadArgs to hold an integer id and a std::string message.
  2. In main, we dynamically allocate an instance of ThreadArgs using new. This is important! If you pass a pointer to a local variable on the main function's stack, that variable might go out of scope and be destroyed before the new thread gets a chance to use it.
  3. We pass the pointer to this struct, cast as void*, to pthread_create.
  4. Inside the printArgs function, we cast the void* argument back to a ThreadArgs* so we can access its members.
  5. After the thread is done with the arguments, it frees the memory allocated in main by calling delete.

Sample Output:

Thread ID: 101, Message: This is a message for the thread.

docs.title: 2. The Power of Parallelism
docs.text: Now, let's explore why using multiple threads can significantly speed up our programs. We'll do this by writing a program to count prime numbers in a given range, first sequentially and then in parallel.

docs.title: Measuring Time Accurately: Monotonic Clocks
docs.text:
To measure the performance of our sequential and parallel code, we need an accurate timer. Not all clocks are suitable for this. For benchmarking, we should use a monotonic clock.

A monotonic clock is a clock that can only move forward. It is not affected by changes to the system's "wall-clock" time, such as a user manually changing the time or automatic adjustments for daylight saving. This property ensures that the time duration we measure between two points is always positive and accurately reflects the elapsed time. In C++, std::chrono::steady_clock is guaranteed to be monotonic and is the best choice for measuring time intervals.

docs.title: The isPrime() Function
docs.text:
We need a function that does a fair amount of work. Checking for prime numbers is a good example.

// A simple function to check if a number is prime
bool isPrime(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return false;
    for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; ++i) {
        if (n % i == 0) return false;
    }
    return true;
}

Algorithm Explanation: This function checks if a number n is prime by iterating from 2 up to the square root of n. If n is divisible by any number in this range, it's not a prime number.

docs.title: The Full Program: Sequential vs. Parallel
docs.text:
The program below will first count primes sequentially and then do it in parallel, finally printing a comparison of the results.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <chrono>
#include <vector>

#define NUM_THREADS 4 // Feel free to change this based on your CPU cores

// isPrime function from above
bool isPrime(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return false;
    for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; ++i) {
        if (n % i == 0) return false;
    }
    return true;
}

// Struct to pass data to our prime counting threads
struct PrimeCounterData {
    int start;
    int end;
    int count;
};

void* countPrimes(void* arg) {
    PrimeCounterData* data = (PrimeCounterData*) arg;
    data->count = 0;
    for (int i = data->start; i < data->end; ++i) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            data->count++;
        }
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    const int N = 200000;

    // --- SEQUENTIAL EXECUTION ---
    std::cout << "--- Sequential Execution ---" << std::endl;
    auto start_time_seq = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

    int sequential_prime_count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            sequential_prime_count++;
        }
    }

    auto end_time_seq = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    std::chrono::duration<double> sequential_time = end_time_seq - start_time_seq;
    std::cout << "Primes found: " << sequential_prime_count << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Time taken: " << sequential_time.count() << " seconds" << std::endl;
    std::cout << std::endl;


    // --- PARALLEL EXECUTION ---
    std::cout << "--- Parallel Execution (" << NUM_THREADS << " threads) ---" << std::endl;
    auto start_time_parallel = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();

    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];
    PrimeCounterData thread_data[NUM_THREADS];
    int total_primes_parallel = 0;

    int chunk_size = N / NUM_THREADS;
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        thread_data[i].start = i * chunk_size;
        thread_data[i].end = (i == NUM_THREADS - 1) ? N : (i + 1) * chunk_size;
        pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, countPrimes, &thread_data[i]);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);
        total_primes_parallel += thread_data[i].count;
    }

    auto end_time_parallel = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    std::chrono::duration<double> parallel_time = end_time_parallel - start_time_parallel;
    std::cout << "Primes found: " << total_primes_parallel << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Time taken: " << parallel_time.count() << " seconds" << std::endl;
    std::cout << std::endl;

    // --- ANALYSIS ---
    std::cout << "--- Analysis ---" << std::endl;
    double speedup = sequential_time.count() / parallel_time.count();
    double efficiency = speedup / NUM_THREADS;
    std::cout << "Speedup: " << speedup << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Efficiency: " << efficiency << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

docs.title: 3. Thread Synchronization
docs.text: When multiple threads access and modify shared data concurrently, it can lead to unpredictable results. This situation is known as a race condition. The part of the code that accesses the shared resource is called the critical section.

docs.title: Demonstrating a Race Condition
docs.text:
Let's look at a simple example where multiple threads increment a shared counter.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

#define NUM_THREADS 10
#define INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD 100000

long long shared_counter = 0;

void* incrementCounter(void* arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD; ++i) {
        shared_counter++; // CRITICAL SECTION
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, incrementCounter, NULL);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);
    }

    std::cout << "Expected counter value: " << (long long)NUM_THREADS * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Actual counter value: " << shared_counter << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

Sample Output (will likely vary with each run):

Expected counter value: 1000000
Actual counter value: 784321

What Went Wrong? The shared_counter++ operation is not atomic. It typically involves three machine-level steps: 1. Read the value of shared_counter from memory into a register. 2. Increment the value in the register. 3. Write the new value back to shared_counter in memory. A race condition occurs when Thread A reads the value, but before it can write the new value back, the scheduler switches to Thread B. Thread B also reads the original value, increments it, and writes it back. When Thread A resumes, it writes its incremented value, overwriting the work done by Thread B. One increment is lost.

docs.title: Fixing the Race Condition with Mutexes
docs.text:
A mutex (mutual exclusion) is a synchronization primitive that acts like a lock. It can be used to protect a critical section, ensuring that only one thread can execute that code at a time.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

#define NUM_THREADS 10
#define INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD 100000

long long shared_counter = 0;
pthread_mutex_t mutex; // Declare the mutex

void* incrementCounter(void* arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD; ++i) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);   // Lock the mutex
        shared_counter++;             // CRITICAL SECTION
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex); // Unlock the mutex
    }
    return NULL;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];

    pthread_mutex_init(&mutex, NULL); // Initialize the mutex

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_create(&threads[i], NULL, incrementCounter, NULL);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], NULL);
    }

    pthread_mutex_destroy(&mutex); // Destroy the mutex

    std::cout << "Expected counter value: " << (long long)NUM_THREADS * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Actual counter value: " << shared_counter << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

Explanation: * pthread_mutex_t mutex;: Declares a mutex variable. * pthread_mutex_init(&mutex, NULL);: Initializes the mutex before use. * pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);: Before entering the critical section, a thread attempts to lock the mutex. If the mutex is already locked by another thread, this thread will block (wait) until the mutex is unlocked. * pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex);: After leaving the critical section, the thread unlocks the mutex, allowing other waiting threads to proceed. * pthread_mutex_destroy(&mutex);: Destroys the mutex when it is no longer needed, freeing up any associated resources.

Sample Output:

Expected counter value: 1000000
Actual counter value: 1000000

docs.title: 1. Thread Creation
docs.text: In this section, you'll learn the basics of creating and managing a new thread of execution within your program.

docs.title: What is a Thread?
docs.text:
A thread is the smallest unit of execution within a process. A single process can have multiple threads running concurrently, all sharing the same memory space (like global variables and the heap). However, each thread has its own private program counter, stack, and set of registers. This shared memory model makes communication between threads efficient but also introduces synchronization challenges.

The main thread of your program starts when main() is called. This main thread can then create other threads. This process is often referred to as forking.

docs.title: Thread Forking and Joining
docs.text:
• Forking: The pthread_create function creates a new thread. After the call, the original (parent) thread and the new (child) thread run concurrently.

    Diagram: Thread Forking 

    graph TD
    A[Main Thread] --> B{pthread_create()};
    B --> C[Main Thread Continues];
    B --> D[New Thread Executes];

  • Joining: A thread can wait for another thread to complete by calling pthread_join. This is a blocking call, pausing the calling thread until the target thread terminates. This is essential for retrieving results computed by a child thread.

    Diagram: Thread Joining 

    graph TD
    subgraph Parallel Execution
        A[Main Thread]
        B[Child Thread]
    end
    A -- Runs Concurrently --> C{pthread_join(child)};
    B -- Runs Concurrently --> D[Finishes Task];
    D --> C;
    C -- Resumes Execution --> E[Main Thread Continues];

docs.title: Creating a Simple Thread
docs.text:
To get started, you must include the pthread.h header file. Let's create a thread that prints a simple message.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

// The function that the new thread will execute.
void* myFirstThread(void* arg) {
    std::cout << "Hello from the new thread!" << std::endl;
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread_id; // Opaque variable to store the thread identifier

    std::cout << "Main thread: Creating a new thread." << std::endl;

    // Create the new thread
    pthread_create(&thread_id, nullptr, myFirstThread, nullptr);

    // Wait for the created thread to finish its execution
    pthread_join(thread_id, nullptr);

    std::cout << "Main thread: The new thread has finished." << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

Explanation:

  • #include <pthread.h>: Includes the Pthread library.
  • nullptr vs NULL: We use nullptr, the modern C++ standard for representing a null pointer, instead of the older C-style NULL macro.
  • pthread_create(&thread_id, nullptr, myFirstThread, nullptr): Creates the thread.
    • 1st argument: A pointer to thread_id to store the thread's identifier.
    • 2nd argument: A pointer to thread attributes; nullptr specifies default attributes.
    • 3rd argument: A pointer to the function the thread will execute.
    • 4th argument: A void* pointer to the argument for the thread function.
  • pthread_join(thread_id, nullptr): The main thread waits here until the thread identified by thread_id completes.

Sample Output:

Main thread: Creating a new thread.
Hello from the new thread!
Main thread: The new thread has finished.

docs.title: Passing Arguments to a Thread
docs.text:
You can pass a single value to a thread by casting a pointer to void*.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

void* printMessage(void* msg) {
    // Cast the void* argument back to its original type
    char* message = (char*) msg;
    std::cout << message << std::endl;
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread1, thread2;
    const char* message1 = "This is thread 1.";
    const char* message2 = "This is thread 2.";

    // Create threads and pass a string literal to each
    pthread_create(&thread1, nullptr, printMessage, (void*) message1);
    pthread_create(&thread2, nullptr, printMessage, (void*) message2);

    // Wait for the threads to finish
    pthread_join(thread1, nullptr);
    pthread_join(thread2, nullptr);

    return 0;
}

Sample Output:

This is thread 1.
This is thread 2.

docs.title: Passing Multiple Values
docs.text:
To pass multiple values, you must bundle them into a struct and pass a pointer to an instance of that struct.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <string>

// A struct to hold multiple arguments for our thread
struct ThreadArgs {
    int id;
    std::string message;
};

void* printArgs(void* arg) {
    // Cast the void* back to our struct type
    ThreadArgs* args = (ThreadArgs*) arg;

    std::cout << "Thread ID: " << args->id
              << ", Message: '" << args->message << "'" << std::endl;

    // Free the dynamically allocated memory to avoid leaks
    delete args;

    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread1;

    // IMPORTANT: Allocate the struct on the heap, not the stack,
    // to ensure it still exists when the new thread accesses it.
    ThreadArgs* args = new ThreadArgs();
    args->id = 101;
    args->message = "Passing multiple values is easy!";

    // Create the thread, passing a pointer to the struct
    pthread_create(&thread1, nullptr, printArgs, (void*) args);
    pthread_join(thread1, nullptr);

    return 0;
}

Sample Output:

Thread ID: 101, Message: 'Passing multiple values is easy!'

docs.title: 2. The Power of Parallelism
docs.text: Now, let's explore why using multiple threads can significantly speed up our programs. We'll do this by writing a program to count prime numbers in a given range, first sequentially and then in parallel.

docs.title: Measuring Time Accurately: Monotonic Clocks
docs.text: To measure the performance of our sequential and parallel code, we need an accurate timer. For benchmarking, we should use a monotonic clock. A monotonic clock is a clock that can only move forward and is not affected by system time changes (like a user manually changing the time or daylight saving adjustments). This property ensures that the time duration we measure between two points is always positive and accurately reflects the elapsed time. In C++, std::chrono::steady_clock is guaranteed to be monotonic and is the best choice for measuring time intervals.

docs.title: The isPrime() Function
docs.text:
We need a function that does a fair amount of work to properly see the benefits of parallelism. Checking for prime numbers is a good example of a CPU-intensive task.

// A simple function to check if a number is prime
bool isPrime(int n) {
    if (n <= 1) return false;
    for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; ++i) {
        if (n % i == 0) return false;
    }
    return true;
}

Algorithm Explanation:

This function checks if a number n is prime by trying to divide it by numbers starting from 2 up to the square root of n. If n is divisible by any number in this range, it cannot be a prime number. We only need to check up to the square root because if a number n has a divisor larger than its square root, it must also have a divisor smaller than it.

docs.title: The Full Program: Sequential vs. Parallel
docs.text:
The program below will first count primes sequentially and then do it in parallel, finally printing a comparison of the results.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <chrono>
#include <vector>

#define NUM_THREADS 4 // Feel free to change this based on your CPU cores

// isPrime function is defined above

// Struct to pass data to our prime counting threads
struct PrimeCounterData {
    int start;
    int end;
    int count;
};

void* countPrimes(void* arg) {
    PrimeCounterData* data = (PrimeCounterData*) arg;
    data->count = 0;
    for (int i = data->start; i < data->end; ++i) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            data->count++;
        }
    }
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    const int N = 200000;

    // --- SEQUENTIAL EXECUTION ---
    std::cout << "--- Sequential Execution ---" << std::endl;
    auto start_time_seq = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    int sequential_prime_count = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < N; ++i) {
        if (isPrime(i)) sequential_prime_count++;
    }
    auto end_time_seq = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    std::chrono::duration<double> sequential_time = end_time_seq - start_time_seq;
    std::cout << "Primes found: " << sequential_prime_count << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Time taken: " << sequential_time.count() << " seconds" << std::endl << std::endl;

    // --- PARALLEL EXECUTION ---
    std::cout << "--- Parallel Execution (" << NUM_THREADS << " threads) ---" << std::endl;
    auto start_time_parallel = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];
    PrimeCounterData thread_data[NUM_THREADS];
    int total_primes_parallel = 0;
    int chunk_size = N / NUM_THREADS;

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        thread_data[i].start = i * chunk_size;
        thread_data[i].end = (i == NUM_THREADS - 1) ? N : (i + 1) * chunk_size;
        pthread_create(&threads[i], nullptr, countPrimes, &thread_data[i]);
    }

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], nullptr);
        total_primes_parallel += thread_data[i].count;
    }

    auto end_time_parallel = std::chrono::steady_clock::now();
    std::chrono::duration<double> parallel_time = end_time_parallel - start_time_parallel;
    std::cout << "Primes found: " << total_primes_parallel << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Time taken: " << parallel_time.count() << " seconds" << std::endl << std::endl;

    // --- ANALYSIS ---
    std::cout << "--- Analysis ---" << std::endl;
    double speedup = sequential_time.count() / parallel_time.count();
    double efficiency = speedup / NUM_THREADS;
    std::cout << "Speedup: " << speedup << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Efficiency: " << efficiency << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

Sample Output (will vary based on your machine):

--- Sequential Execution ---
Primes found: 17984
Time taken: 0.234567 seconds

--- Parallel Execution (4 threads) ---
Primes found: 17984
Time taken: 0.061234 seconds

--- Analysis ---
Speedup: 3.8309
Efficiency: 0.9577

docs.title: 3. Thread Synchronization
docs.text: When multiple threads access and modify shared data concurrently, it can lead to unpredictable results. This situation is known as a race condition. The section of code accessing the shared resource is called the critical section.

docs.title: Demonstrating a Race Condition
docs.text:
Let's look at a simple example where multiple threads increment a shared counter without any protection.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

#define NUM_THREADS 10
#define INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD 100000

long long shared_counter = 0;

void* incrementCounter(void* arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD; ++i) {
        shared_counter++; // RACE CONDITION HERE!
    }
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_create(&threads[i], nullptr, incrementCounter, nullptr);
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], nullptr);
    }

    std::cout << "Expected counter value: " << (long long)NUM_THREADS * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Actual counter value:   " << shared_counter << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

Sample Output (will likely vary with each run):

Expected counter value: 1000000
Actual counter value:   784321

What Went Wrong? The shared_counter++ operation is not atomic; it's a sequence of read-modify-write. A race condition occurs when one thread reads the counter's value, but before it can write the new value back, the scheduler switches to another thread. That thread also reads the same original value. Both threads write back an incremented value, but one of the updates is lost.

docs.title: Fixing the Race Condition with Mutexes
docs.text:
A mutex (mutual exclusion) is a synchronization primitive that acts like a lock. It can be used to protect a critical section, ensuring that only one thread can execute that code at a time.

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

#define NUM_THREADS 10
#define INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD 100000

long long shared_counter = 0;
pthread_mutex_t mutex; // Declare the mutex

void* incrementCounter(void* arg) {
    for (int i = 0; i < INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD; ++i) {
        pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex);   // Lock the mutex
        shared_counter++;             // CRITICAL SECTION
        pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex); // Unlock the mutex
    }
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];

    pthread_mutex_init(&mutex, nullptr); // Initialize the mutex

    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_create(&threads[i], nullptr, incrementCounter, nullptr);
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; ++i) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], nullptr);
    }

    pthread_mutex_destroy(&mutex); // Destroy the mutex

    std::cout << "Expected counter value: " << (long long)NUM_THREADS * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Actual counter value:   " << shared_counter << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

Explanation: * pthread_mutex_init(&mutex, nullptr): Initializes the mutex before use. * pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex): A thread attempts to acquire the lock. If another thread holds it, this thread will wait (block). * pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex): The thread releases the lock, allowing another waiting thread to proceed. * pthread_mutex_destroy(&mutex): Frees any resources associated with the mutex when it is no longer needed.

Sample Output:

Expected counter value: 1000000
Actual counter value:   1000000

Introduction
docs.text: Welcome to this comprehensive tutorial on the Pthread (POSIX Threads) library in C++. In this lab, you'll learn the fundamentals of thread creation and understand why thread synchronization is crucial in multithreaded programming. By the end of this tutorial, you'll be able to create threads, pass data between them, and understand the challenges that arise when threads work together.

• Basic knowledge of C++ programming
  • Understanding of functions and pointers
  • Familiarity with compilation using g++

docs.title: Compilation Instructions
docs.text:
Throughout this tutorial, compile your programs using: 

g++ -pthread -o program_name source_file.cpp

The -pthread flag links the pthread library to your program.

docs.title: 1.1 Basic Thread Creation
docs.text:
Let's start with the most fundamental concept: creating and managing threads.

Key Functions: - pthread_create(): Creates a new thread - pthread_join(): Waits for a thread to complete - pthread_exit(): Terminates the current thread

Basic Syntax: 

int pthread_create(pthread_t *thread, const pthread_attr_t *attr,
                   void *(*start_routine)(void *), void *arg);
int pthread_join(pthread_t thread, void **retval);

Let's create our first threaded program:

Example 1.1: Basic Thread Creation

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <unistd.h>

// Thread function - this is what the thread will execute
void* threadFunction(void* arg) {
    std::cout << "Hello from thread! Thread ID: " << pthread_self() << std::endl;

    // Simulate some work
    sleep(2);

    std::cout << "Thread finishing execution" << std::endl;
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    pthread_t thread;

    std::cout << "Main thread starting. Main thread ID: " << pthread_self() << std::endl;

    // Create the thread
    int result = pthread_create(&thread, nullptr, threadFunction, nullptr);

    if (result != 0) {
        std::cerr << "Error creating thread!" << std::endl;
        return 1;
    }

    std::cout << "Thread created successfully" << std::endl;

    // Wait for the thread to complete
    pthread_join(thread, nullptr);

    std::cout << "Main thread ending" << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

What's happening here?

  1. We define a thread function threadFunction() that takes a void* parameter and returns void*
  2. In main(), we declare a pthread_t variable to hold the thread identifier
  3. pthread_create() creates the thread with default attributes (nullptr)
  4. pthread_join() makes the main thread wait for the worker thread to finish
  5. Both threads have unique IDs that we can print using pthread_self()

Expected Output: 

Main thread starting. Main thread ID: [some number]
Thread created successfully
Hello from thread! Thread ID: [different number]
Thread finishing execution
Main thread ending

docs.title: 1.2 Thread with Parameters
docs.text:
Now let's learn how to pass data to threads. Since pthread_create() accepts only a void* parameter, we need to use structures to pass multiple values.

Example 1.2: Passing Data to Threads

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <string>

// Structure to hold thread parameters
struct ThreadData {
    int id;
    std::string message;
    int count;
};

// Thread function that uses the passed data
void* threadFunction(void* arg) {
    // Cast the void* back to our structure
    ThreadData* data = static_cast<ThreadData*>(arg);

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->id << " started" << std::endl;

    // Use the data passed to the thread
    for (int i = 0; i < data->count; i++) {
        std::cout << "Thread " << data->id << ": " << data->message 
                  << " (iteration " << (i + 1) << ")" << std::endl;
    }

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->id << " finished" << std::endl;
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    const int NUM_THREADS = 3;
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];
    ThreadData threadData[NUM_THREADS];

    std::cout << "Creating " << NUM_THREADS << " threads..." << std::endl;

    // Create multiple threads with different data
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        threadData[i].id = i + 1;
        threadData[i].message = "Hello from thread " + std::to_string(i + 1);
        threadData[i].count = (i + 1) * 2;  // Different work load for each thread

        int result = pthread_create(&threads[i], nullptr, threadFunction, &threadData[i]);

        if (result != 0) {
            std::cerr << "Error creating thread " << i << std::endl;
            return 1;
        }
    }

    // Wait for all threads to complete
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], nullptr);
    }

    std::cout << "All threads completed!" << std::endl;
    return 0;
}

Key Points: - We use a struct to package multiple parameters - Each thread gets its own copy of the data structure - We cast void* back to our structure type inside the thread function - Multiple threads can run concurrently, so output order may vary

docs.title: 2.1 Understanding the isPrime() Algorithm
docs.text:
Before we dive into parallel programming, let's understand our example algorithm. We'll use prime number checking because it's computationally intensive and naturally parallelizable.

Prime Number Checking Algorithm:

bool isPrime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return false;
    if (n == 2) return true;
    if (n % 2 == 0) return false;

    // Check odd divisors up to sqrt(n)
    for (int i = 3; i * i <= n; i += 2) {
        if (n % i == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

Why is this good for parallelism? 1. Independent computations: Checking if number X is prime doesn't depend on checking number Y 2. CPU-intensive: Lots of mathematical operations that can benefit from parallel processing 3. Scalable workload: We can easily divide the range of numbers among multiple threads

docs.title: 2.2 Simple Sequential Example
docs.text:
Let's establish our baseline with a sequential (single-threaded) implementation:

Example 2.2: Sequential Prime Counting

#include <iostream>
#include <chrono>

bool isPrime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return false;
    if (n == 2) return true;
    if (n % 2 == 0) return false;

    for (int i = 3; i * i <= n; i += 2) {
        if (n % i == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

int countPrimesSequential(int start, int end) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = start; i <= end; i++) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main() {
    const int START = 1;
    const int END = 100000;

    std::cout << "Counting primes from " << START << " to " << END << " (sequential)" << std::endl;

    // Measure execution time
    auto start_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();

    int primeCount = countPrimesSequential(START, END);

    auto end_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    auto duration = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(end_time - start_time);

    std::cout << "Found " << primeCount << " prime numbers" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Sequential execution time: " << duration.count() << " milliseconds" << std::endl;

    return 0;
}

Run this program and note the execution time. This will be our baseline for comparison.

docs.title: 2.3 Parallelism Example
docs.text: Now let's harness the power of multiple threads to speed up our computation!

docs.title: 2.3.1 countPrimesSequential() Analysis
docs.text: Our sequential function processes numbers one by one in a single thread: - Input: Range of numbers (start to end) - Process: Check each number individually - Output: Count of prime numbers - Limitation: Uses only one CPU core

docs.title: 2.3.2 countPrimesParallel() Components
docs.text:
To parallelize this, we need three key components:

Component 1: Thread Data Structure 

struct ThreadData {
    int start;        // Starting number for this thread
    int end;          // Ending number for this thread
    int result;       // Store the count of primes found
    int threadId;     // For identification and debugging
};

Component 2: Thread Function 

void* countPrimesThread(void* arg) {
    ThreadData* data = static_cast<ThreadData*>(arg);

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId 
              << " processing range [" << data->start 
              << ", " << data->end << "]" << std::endl;

    data->result = 0;
    for (int i = data->start; i <= data->end; i++) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            data->result++;
        }
    }

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId 
              << " found " << data->result << " primes" << std::endl;

    return nullptr;
}

Component 3: Work Distribution Strategy 

// Divide the work evenly among threads
int rangeSize = (END - START + 1) / NUM_THREADS;
for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
    threadData[i].start = START + i * rangeSize;
    threadData[i].end = (i == NUM_THREADS - 1) ? END : threadData[i].start + rangeSize - 1;
    threadData[i].threadId = i;
}

docs.title: 2.3.3 Complete Parallel Program
docs.text:
Example 2.3: Parallel Prime Counting

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>
#include <chrono>

struct ThreadData {
    int start;
    int end;
    int result;
    int threadId;
};

bool isPrime(int n) {
    if (n < 2) return false;
    if (n == 2) return true;
    if (n % 2 == 0) return false;

    for (int i = 3; i * i <= n; i += 2) {
        if (n % i == 0) {
            return false;
        }
    }
    return true;
}

void* countPrimesThread(void* arg) {
    ThreadData* data = static_cast<ThreadData*>(arg);

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId 
              << " processing range [" << data->start 
              << ", " << data->end << "]" << std::endl;

    data->result = 0;
    for (int i = data->start; i <= data->end; i++) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            data->result++;
        }
    }

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId 
              << " found " << data->result << " primes" << std::endl;

    return nullptr;
}

int countPrimesParallel(int start, int end, int numThreads) {
    pthread_t* threads = new pthread_t[numThreads];
    ThreadData* threadData = new ThreadData[numThreads];

    // Distribute work among threads
    int rangeSize = (end - start + 1) / numThreads;

    std::cout << "Creating " << numThreads << " threads for parallel processing..." << std::endl;

    // Create threads
    for (int i = 0; i < numThreads; i++) {
        threadData[i].start = start + i * rangeSize;
        threadData[i].end = (i == numThreads - 1) ? end : threadData[i].start + rangeSize - 1;
        threadData[i].threadId = i;
        threadData[i].result = 0;

        int result = pthread_create(&threads[i], nullptr, countPrimesThread, &threadData[i]);
        if (result != 0) {
            std::cerr << "Error creating thread " << i << std::endl;
            return -1;
        }
    }

    // Wait for all threads to complete
    for (int i = 0; i < numThreads; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], nullptr);
    }

    // Combine results from all threads
    int totalPrimes = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < numThreads; i++) {
        totalPrimes += threadData[i].result;
    }

    delete[] threads;
    delete[] threadData;

    return totalPrimes;
}

// Sequential version for comparison
int countPrimesSequential(int start, int end) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int i = start; i <= end; i++) {
        if (isPrime(i)) {
            count++;
        }
    }
    return count;
}

int main() {
    const int START = 1;
    const int END = 100000;
    const int NUM_THREADS = 4;

    std::cout << "=== Prime Number Counting Performance Comparison ===" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Range: " << START << " to " << END << std::endl << std::endl;

    // Sequential execution
    std::cout << "1. Sequential Execution:" << std::endl;
    auto start_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    int sequentialResult = countPrimesSequential(START, END);
    auto end_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    auto sequentialDuration = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(end_time - start_time);

    std::cout << "Found " << sequentialResult << " prime numbers" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Sequential time: " << sequentialDuration.count() << " ms" << std::endl << std::endl;

    // Parallel execution
    std::cout << "2. Parallel Execution (" << NUM_THREADS << " threads):" << std::endl;
    start_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    int parallelResult = countPrimesParallel(START, END, NUM_THREADS);
    end_time = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
    auto parallelDuration = std::chrono::duration_cast<std::chrono::milliseconds>(end_time - start_time);

    std::cout << "Found " << parallelResult << " prime numbers" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Parallel time: " << parallelDuration.count() << " ms" << std::endl << std::endl;

    // Performance analysis
    std::cout << "=== Performance Analysis ===" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Correctness check: " << (sequentialResult == parallelResult ? "PASSED" : "FAILED") << std::endl;

    if (parallelDuration.count() > 0) {
        double speedup = static_cast<double>(sequentialDuration.count()) / parallelDuration.count();
        std::cout << "Speedup: " << speedup << "x" << std::endl;
        std::cout << "Efficiency: " << (speedup / NUM_THREADS) * 100 << "%" << std::endl;
    }

    return 0;
}

Expected Output Analysis:

When you run this program, you should see: 1. Correctness: Both methods should find the same number of primes 2. Performance: The parallel version should be faster (speedup depends on your CPU) 3. Thread Activity: You'll see each thread reporting its assigned range and results

Try experimenting with different values: - Change NUM_THREADS (try 2, 4, 8) - Change the range (try 1 to 50000 or 1 to 200000) - Observe how performance changes

docs.title: Conceptual Foundation
docs.text:
So far, our threads have worked independently—each thread processed its own range of numbers without interacting with others. This worked well because: - Each thread had its own data - No thread needed to access shared resources - Results were combined only after all threads finished

However, in many real-world scenarios, threads need to: - Share data structures (arrays, lists, counters) - Access shared resources (files, network connections) - Coordinate their activities

docs.title: Critical Section Concept
docs.text:
A critical section is a code segment where threads access shared resources. Problems arise when multiple threads enter the critical section simultaneously.

Example of a Critical Section: 

// Shared variable
int globalCounter = 0;

// Critical section - accessing shared variable
void incrementCounter() {
    globalCounter++;  // This is NOT atomic!
}

The increment operation globalCounter++ actually involves three steps: 1. Read the current value of globalCounter 2. Add 1 to that value 3. Write the new value back to globalCounter

If two threads execute these steps simultaneously, we can lose updates!

docs.title: Overview of Synchronization Mechanisms
docs.text:
Mutex (Mutual Exclusion): - Ensures only one thread can access a critical section at a time - Like a lock on a bathroom door

Semaphore: - Controls access to a resource with limited capacity - Like a parking lot with limited spaces

Condition Variables: - Allow threads to wait for certain conditions - Like waiting for a signal to proceed

In this tutorial, we'll focus on mutex as it's the most fundamental synchronization mechanism.

docs.title: Part 4: The Problem - Race Conditions
docs.text: Let's demonstrate why synchronization is necessary by creating a program that exhibits race conditions.

docs.title: Race Condition Demonstration
docs.text:
Example 4.1: The Broken Counter

#include <iostream>
#include <pthread.h>

// Shared global variable - THIS IS THE PROBLEM!
int globalCounter = 0;
const int INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD = 100000;

struct ThreadData {
    int threadId;
};

void* incrementCounter(void* arg) {
    ThreadData* data = static_cast<ThreadData*>(arg);

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId << " starting to increment..." << std::endl;

    // Each thread increments the counter many times
    for (int i = 0; i < INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD; i++) {
        globalCounter++;  // RACE CONDITION: Multiple threads accessing globalCounter
    }

    std::cout << "Thread " << data->threadId << " finished incrementing" << std::endl;
    return nullptr;
}

int main() {
    const int NUM_THREADS = 4;
    pthread_t threads[NUM_THREADS];
    ThreadData threadData[NUM_THREADS];

    std::cout << "=== Race Condition Demonstration ===" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Expected final value: " << (NUM_THREADS * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD) << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Initial counter value: " << globalCounter << std::endl << std::endl;

    // Create threads
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        threadData[i].threadId = i;
        pthread_create(&threads[i], nullptr, incrementCounter, &threadData[i]);
    }

    // Wait for all threads to complete
    for (int i = 0; i < NUM_THREADS; i++) {
        pthread_join(threads[i], nullptr);
    }

    std::cout << std::endl << "=== Results ===" << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Final counter value: " << globalCounter << std::endl;
    std::cout << "Expected value: " << (NUM_THREADS * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD) << std::endl;

    if (globalCounter == (NUM_THREADS * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD)) {
        std::cout << "Result: CORRECT (lucky!)" << std::endl;
    } else {
        std::cout << "Result: INCORRECT - Race condition occurred!" << std::endl;
        std::cout << "Lost updates: " << (NUM_THREADS * INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD) - globalCounter << std::endl;
    }

    return 0;
}

docs.title: Analysis: What Goes Wrong and Why
docs.text:
Run this program multiple times. You'll likely see different results each time, and the final counter value will often be less than expected.

Why does this happen?

  1. The increment operation globalCounter++ is not atomic: 

    Thread A: Read globalCounter (value = 100)
Thread B: Read globalCounter (value = 100)  ← Same value!
Thread A: Calculate 100 + 1 = 101
Thread B: Calculate 100 + 1 = 101          ← Same calculation!
Thread A: Write 101 to globalCounter
Thread B: Write 101 to globalCounter       ← Overwrites A's work!

  2. Lost updates: When two threads read the same value and both increment it, one increment is lost.

  3. Non-deterministic behavior: The timing of thread execution is unpredictable, leading to different results each run.

Try running the program with different parameters: - Reduce INCREMENTS_PER_THREAD to 1000 - does the problem still occur? - Increase NUM_THREADS to 8 - does the problem get worse? - Add sleep() calls in the loop - how does this affect the race condition?

docs.title: Understanding the Race Window
docs.text:
The "race window" is the time between reading a shared variable and writing back to it. The longer this window, the more likely race conditions become.

// Wider race window
int temp = globalCounter;  // Step 1: Read
temp = temp + 1;          // Step 2: Modify  
globalCounter = temp;     // Step 3: Write
// More time for another thread to interfere!

// Narrower race window
globalCounter++;          // All three steps together
// Still not atomic, but smaller window

docs.title: Summary: Why We Need Synchronization
docs.text:
This demonstration shows that even simple operations like incrementing a counter can go wrong in multithreaded environments. We need synchronization mechanisms to:

  1. Ensure atomicity: Operations on shared data complete without interference
  2. Prevent race conditions: Control access to critical sections
  3. Maintain data consistency: Ensure shared data remains in a valid state
  4. Provide predictable behavior: Make multithreaded programs deterministic

In the next part of this tutorial series, we'll learn how to fix these problems using mutex locks and other synchronization techniques.
